section.title: Stand Firm
section.sectionRationale: After the sobering account of the man of lawlessness and those who perish, Paul turns to the church with thanksgiving and comfort. Over against the deceived stand the beloved, whom God chose from the beginning for salvation through the Spirit and faith in the truth. Therefore they are to stand firm and hold the apostolic teaching, upheld by a prayer that the Lord and the Father would strengthen their hearts. This short movement is the reassuring counterpart to the warning that precedes it.
section.thesis: Because God chose the Thessalonians from the beginning and called them through the gospel to share Christ's glory, they can and must stand firm and hold fast the truth they were taught, resting in the God who by grace gives eternal comfort and strengthens His people for every good word and deed.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the thanksgiving for God's electing, calling, saving work that sets the beloved apart from the perishing, with the resulting command to stand firm and hold the traditions; and the benediction that grounds their steadfastness in the comforting, strengthening grace of the Lord Jesus and the Father.

verses.text: But we should always thank God for you, brothers who are loved by the Lord, because God {{haireomai|chose}} you from the beginning to be saved by the {{hagiasmos|sanctification}} of the Spirit and by faith in the truth.
To this He called you through our gospel, so that you may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, brothers, {{steko|stand firm}} and cling to the {{paradosis|traditions}} we taught you, whether by speech or by letter.

units.label: Benediction of comfort and strength
units.note: the Lord and the Father encourage and strengthen

verses.text: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and God our Father, who by grace has loved us and given us eternal {{paraklesis|comfort}} and good hope,
encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good word and deed.

haireomai.gloss: To choose, select, take for oneself. Paul says God chose the Thessalonians from the beginning for salvation, an act of God's free love that stands behind their faith. The middle voice underlines that God took them to be His own, so their standing rests on His choice, not their strength.

hagiasmos.gloss: Sanctification, the process of being made holy and set apart for God. Here it is the Spirit's work, paired with faith in the truth, as the means by which God's chosen are saved. Salvation is not bare pardon but a real setting apart, begun and carried on by the Holy Spirit.

steko.gloss: To stand firm, hold one's ground, remain steadfast. Built from the verb to stand, it pictures a soldier or a settled person who will not be moved. Because God has chosen and called them, the command is not to muster their own courage but to keep standing in the truth they have received.

paradosis.gloss: Tradition, that which is handed over or passed on. Here it means the apostolic teaching Paul delivered, whether spoken or written, not later human inventions. To hold the traditions is to cling to the authoritative gospel and instruction the apostles gave, the anchor against every deceiving message.

paraklesis.gloss: Comfort, encouragement, exhortation; a calling alongside to help. Paul says the Lord and the Father have given eternal comfort by grace, and prays that this comfort would steady their hearts. It is not fleeting reassurance but a lasting encouragement rooted in God's love and good hope.

basic.context: Having just described those who perish because they refused the truth, Paul turns to the church with relief and gratitude. You are different, he says: God loved you and chose you from the beginning to be saved, set apart by the Spirit and holding faith in the truth, and He called you through the gospel to share in Christ's glory. So the response is simple and strong: stand firm and hold on to what you were taught. Then he prays that God Himself would comfort and strengthen them.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul grounds the command to stand firm in God's prior choosing and calling, so human perseverance rests on divine grace, not the reverse. God's election does not cancel faith and sanctification but works through them; the passage names both God's choice and their faith in the truth. The traditions to be held are specifically apostolic teaching, spoken or written, not any later human custom.
basic.originalLanguages: God haireomai, chose, the Thessalonians from the beginning, an act of free love. Their salvation comes by the hagiasmos of the Spirit, the Spirit's setting apart, together with faith in the truth. Therefore they must steko, stand firm, and hold the paradosis, the apostolic traditions handed down by speech or letter. The benediction rests on paraklesis, the eternal comfort God has given by grace.
basic.typology: God choosing a people from the beginning and setting them apart by His Spirit echoes His election of Israel as His treasured people, set apart to be holy. The church is the chosen and sanctified people, now called through the gospel to share the glory of the Lord Jesus.
basic.christ: Christ is the goal of God's choosing: He called them through the gospel so that they may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. And in the benediction, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself stands alongside God the Father as the source of comfort and strength, named first, and joined with the Father under a single verb, a quiet witness to His deity.
basic.god: God is the loving Chooser and faithful Caller. He loved this church, chose them from the beginning, and called them to glory, and by grace He gives eternal comfort and good hope. The God who elects is the God who then strengthens His people for every good word and deed, so His grace both begins and sustains the Christian life.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 1 says God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy. First Thessalonians 5 urges the same church to encourage and build one another up. And 1 Peter 1 speaks of a people chosen and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience, the same pattern of election through sanctification.
basic.oneStory: The gospel is the story of a God who chooses, calls, sanctifies, and keeps a people for His glory. Set against the ruin of those who refused the truth, the beloved are held secure by God's prior love, called to share the glory of Christ, and strengthened by grace to stand firm to the end.

context.literary:
Verses 13 to 17 are built as a hinge. Verse 13 opens with a sharp contrast: 'But we should always thank God for you.' The 'we' and 'you' are set against the 'they' of verses 10 to 12, and the grammar even echoes the earlier verses. Those who perish refused 'the love of the truth' and 'disbelieved the truth' (verses 10 and 12), while the Thessalonians are saved 'by faith in the truth' (verse 13). The same word is on both sides of the line, and what separates the two groups is what each did with it.

The thanksgiving is one long sentence that runs from eternity to glory. It begins 'from the beginning,' passes through the Spirit's setting apart and the church's faith, moves to the call through the gospel, and ends in sharing Christ's glory. Then comes the single command that all of this supports, in verse 15, introduced by 'Therefore': stand firm and hold on. The prayer wish in verses 16 and 17 then does for the church what the command asks of it. Paul commands them to stand and then asks God to strengthen them.

The section also echoes the very first chapter. There Paul gave thanks for their growing faith (1:3); here he gives thanks for the foundation under it. Together the thanksgivings of 1:3 and 2:13 mark off the great argument about the day of the Lord, so that the letter's teaching on judgment and on the end sits inside gratitude.
context.historical:
The young church in Thessalonica had been founded after a few weeks of preaching (Acts 17:1 to 9) and then chased out of the city by an angry crowd. Many of the believers were Gentiles who had 'turned to God from idols' (1 Thessalonians 1:9), so they had no Scripture-shaped background to fall back on, and their identity as a people was brand new. A letter that tells them they were chosen and called is addressed to a group who were being told by their neighbors that they had walked away from their gods and their city's loyalties and were nobodies.

The word 'traditions' needs to be heard in its first-century setting. In the Jewish world, tradition meant the handing down of a teaching from teacher to student, and the word could carry negative weight when it meant human additions to God's law (Mark 7:8 to 9). Paul uses it positively of the message he himself had received and passed on. In 1 Corinthians 11:2 he praises the Corinthians for 'maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on,' and in 1 Corinthians 15:3 he says he handed on what he had received. In the church's first years, apostolic teaching reached people in two forms, spoken and written, and Paul names both: 'by speech or by letter.'

The mention of letters has a sharper edge here than it would elsewhere, because 2:2 warned about a letter 'seeming to be from us.' By telling them to hold the teaching they received in either form, Paul gives them a standard against which to measure any new letter or prophecy: does it match what the apostles handed on?
context.canonical:
The language of this paragraph is drawn straight from Israel's story of election. Deuteronomy 7:6 to 8 speaks of a people 'holy to the LORD' whom He chose, not because they were many but 'because the LORD loved you.' Paul gives the church the same pattern: beloved by the Lord, chosen, set apart. Peter does the same, addressing the scattered church as 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ' (1 Peter 1:1 to 2), with the Trinity, election, sanctification and obedience in one sentence, just as here.

Within Paul's letters the chain of verses 13 and 14 is a short version of Romans 8:29 to 30, where those God foreknew He predestined, called, justified and glorified. The same chain appears in Ephesians 1:4, where He 'chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless.' The first letter to Thessalonica had already said, 'we know that He has chosen you' (1 Thessalonians 1:4), and gave the evidence: the gospel came 'in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction.'

The command to 'stand firm' belongs to a small family of apostolic exhortations: 'Stand firm in the faith' (1 Corinthians 16:13), 'stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery' (Galatians 5:1), 'stand firm in one spirit' (Philippians 1:27). The call to hold the teaching has a close partner in 2 Timothy 1:13, 'Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching,' and in Jude 3, to 'contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints.' The final prayer takes up Isaiah's 'Comfort, comfort My people' (Isaiah 40:1) in the new covenant.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's aim is to turn a frightening section into a secure one. A church that has just heard about deception and judgment could easily ask, 'Are we safe?' Paul answers by pointing, not to the believers' grip on God, but to God's grip on them. Their security rests on something that happened before they believed and will go on after their faith is tested: the Lord's love, His choosing, His call, and the Spirit's work. He wants them to see their lives as a story that God started and will finish.

He also wants this knowledge to produce action rather than ease. The word 'Therefore' in verse 15 is the hinge. Because they are chosen and called, they must stand firm. He does not set election against effort or effort against election; he lets one produce the other. Election is the ground of perseverance, not an excuse for relaxing.

Finally Paul wants them to have an anchor against confusing voices. He tells them to cling to the teaching they received from him, in speech and letter, so that they would have a standard when someone claims a new revelation. Then he turns from instruction to prayer, which is itself part of the message: the strength to stand is something that has to be asked of God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The first half of the paragraph describes what God has done: He loved, chose, called, sanctified and gave. There is no command in verses 13 and 14, only thanksgiving and truth. The commands begin with verse 15, and they are two: stand firm, and hold on to the teaching. Verses 16 and 17 are neither description nor command but prayer, a request for what only God can supply.

It is important to keep these in order. Treating the description as a command would turn a gift into a burden: the Thessalonians are not told to choose themselves. Treating the commands as optional would turn a gift into a license. In practice this means that believers should draw security from God's work and then obey from that security, not for it.

The 'traditions' are the teaching the apostles handed on in person and in writing, and the command to hold them cannot be used to defend a custom that was added later. The text itself limits the traditions to what was taught 'by speech or by letter,' meaning from Paul and his circle. Whatever its force for later church practice, this verse binds us to the apostolic message, which for us is preserved in the New Testament writings.

debates.question: How does 'God chose you from the beginning to be saved' relate to human faith?

views.label: Unconditional election, with faith as its fruit
views.case: The verse says God chose them 'from the beginning,' before they were born, to be saved, and links Romans 8:29 to 30 and Ephesians 1:4 to 5, which speak of predestination in love. Faith is the means through which the chosen are brought in, and the verse itself says election is 'by' sanctification and faith, not on the basis of foreseen faith. This is the view of Augustine and, after him, the Reformers.

views.label: Election based on God's foreknowledge of faith
views.case: Romans 8:29 says God chose those He 'foreknew,' and 1 Peter 1:2 says 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God.' Some take this to mean God foresaw who would believe and chose them on that basis. The 'faith in the truth' of verse 13 is then read as the condition that God foresaw.

views.label: Corporate election in Christ
views.case: Others read election as God's choice of a people in Christ, so that individuals share in it by being joined to Him through faith. The Old Testament pattern is that God chose Israel as a nation, and the language in verse 13 is plural throughout.

debates.bearing: The text holds God's initiative and the church's faith together and does not explain how they fit. Whatever view one takes, Paul's use is pastoral: election is a reason for thanksgiving and for steadiness, never for pride or for passivity. No reader of verse 13 is encouraged to go and look for whether he is chosen; he is told to believe the truth and to stand.

debates.question: What are 'the traditions' in verse 15, and do they include more than the New Testament?

views.label: The apostolic teaching, now preserved in Scripture
views.case: Paul defines the traditions as what was taught 'by speech or by letter,' which means his own word. Once the apostles died, the only reliable form of that word is the writings that carry their authority. On this view the verse supports the sufficiency of Scripture: whatever the apostles handed on is found in the New Testament.

views.label: Apostolic teaching preserved in Scripture and in the church's living handing on
views.case: The verse names an oral channel alongside the written one, and the early church treated the creeds, the rule of faith and the practice of worship as part of what was handed on. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions argue that the apostles' oral teaching continued in the church. Those traditions say the verse itself shows that not everything was written.

views.label: A particular body of teaching, not later customs
views.case: Others emphasise that the word here is bounded by 'we taught you.' It cannot cover later additions, however valuable. Jesus condemned traditions of men that set aside the commandment of God (Mark 7:8 to 9), so the test is always whether a practice rests on the apostles.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the traditions Paul has in mind came from the apostles, that the church is to hold them tightly, and that the New Testament is the sure written form of them. They differ on whether anything of apostolic authority lies outside it. What the verse requires of everyone is the same: measure every new claim by what the apostles taught.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with a textual question that the Bible's own footnote flags in verse 13. Most manuscripts read that God chose you 'from the beginning,' ap' arches. Some important ones read aparchen, 'as firstfruits,' which gives 'God chose you as the firstfruits for salvation.' The two forms differ by a few letters. Both ideas are Pauline and both are true, since the Thessalonians were an early harvest in Macedonia and God's choice precedes time. But 'from the beginning' fits better with the contrast with verses 10 to 12 and is the reading the Bible prints in its text.

The verb 'chose' is haireomai, a word that means to take for oneself or to select. It is the language of free preference. It is joined to the rare, warm phrase 'loved by the Lord,' agapemenoi hypo kyriou, a perfect participle, meaning loved and remaining loved. The perfect tense says that the love was shown in the past and continues.

The means of salvation is given in one phrase, 'by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth,' with a single preposition governing both nouns. Paul does not treat sanctification and faith as two steps but as two sides of one event. The genitive 'of the Spirit' can mean the Spirit's act of setting apart or the sphere the Spirit creates, and both are included. 'Faith in the truth' is most naturally an objective genitive: faith whose object is the truth, the very truth the perishing rejected.

Verse 14 uses the verb 'called,' ekalesen, in the aorist, a single act of God, and names the instrument, 'our gospel.' The goal is peripoiesis doxes, literally the 'acquiring' or 'obtaining' of glory. Paul uses the noun in 1 Thessalonians 5:9 for obtaining salvation, and the translation 'share in' reflects that the glory is received, not earned.

In verse 15 the imperatives are present tense, steko and krateo. 'Stand firm,' stekete, is a verb Paul uses for steady standing in the Lord (1 Thessalonians 3:8). Krateo means to grip or hold fast. The tradition itself is the paradosis, a noun built from paradidomi, 'to hand over,' the same verb Paul uses for the gospel handed to him in 1 Corinthians 15:3.

The prayer in verses 16 and 17 has a grammatical detail that repays attention. There are two subjects, 'our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and God our Father,' but the verbs 'encourage' and 'strengthen' are both singular. The two aorist participles, 'loved' and 'gave,' are also singular and attach to 'God our Father.' The nouns are paraklesis aionios, eternal comfort or encouragement, the root of the word for 'Advocate' in John 14:16, and elpis agathe, good hope. 'Hope' in the New Testament is not wishing but confident expectation of what God has promised.

typology.type: Israel as God's chosen and holy people
typology.fulfillment: Deuteronomy 7:6 to 8 tells Israel that they were holy to the LORD, chosen not for their size but because the LORD loved them. The Thessalonians are described in the same terms: beloved, chosen, set apart. The correspondence is the order of grace, where love comes first and holiness follows. The escalation in Christ is that the chosen people now gather from every nation and are chosen 'in Him' (Ephesians 1:4), and Peter applies Israel's titles to the church in 1 Peter 2:9. The type falls short in that Israel's holiness was a national and ritual setting apart, while the Spirit's sanctification works inwardly, in the heart.

If the alternate reading in the footnote is right, Paul calls the Thessalonians 'firstfruits.' In Israel the first sheaf of the harvest was presented to the LORD as a pledge of the whole (Leviticus 23:10). In the New Testament Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20), and believers are a kind of firstfruits of God's new creation (James 1:18). The escalation is that the pledge is a living person and a living people. The type falls short in that an Israelite's offering was a sheaf of grain, while here the offering is persons who have become the guarantee of a global harvest.

typology.type: The comfort that follows the exile
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 40:1 opens the book's second half with a double command: 'Comfort, comfort My people.' The comfort is that the God who judged will come and rescue. Paul's 'eternal comfort and good hope' draws on that tradition, with a new foundation. The correspondence is a God who consoles by action, not just by words. The escalation is that the comfort is now eternal and is given through the Lord Jesus and the Spirit, called by John 'another Advocate' (John 14:16). The type falls short in that Isaiah's comfort concerned return from Babylon, a historical rescue that left the deeper exile of sin untouched.

typology.type: The handing on of the covenant words
typology.fulfillment: Moses commanded Israel to impress God's words on their children and to keep them in their hearts (Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7). The Thessalonians are told to cling to what was handed down to them. The pattern is a community defined by a received word that it must pass on. The escalation is that the word handed on is now the gospel, and the apostles who delivered it did so with the Spirit's authority (John 16:13). The type falls short in that Deuteronomy's words were given at one mountain to one nation, while the gospel goes out to the world by speech and letter.

study.christ:
This short paragraph is saturated with Christ in a way that is easy to miss. Notice first how often He is named: 'the Lord' in verse 13, 'our Lord Jesus Christ' in verses 14 and 16. The believers are 'brothers who are loved by the Lord' (the Lord there is Christ), which means that the love they rest on is the love of the One who gave Himself for them (Galatians 2:20). The chain of verses 13 and 14, chosen, sanctified, called, ends not in security as an end in itself but in 'the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.' In Romans 8:29 the destiny is to be 'conformed to the image of His Son,' and in John 17:22 Jesus says, 'I have given them the glory You gave Me.' The goal of election is that the people of God share the glory of the Son.

The second place Christ appears is in the prayer, and it carries a quiet claim about who He is. Paul prays to the Lord Jesus Christ, named first, and God our Father, together, and then uses a singular verb. A Jewish monotheist would not pray to a second being as a partner, and he certainly would not name Him first. Yet Paul does this without argument, as if it were obvious, and he does the same in 1 Thessalonians 3:11 to 13. In 2 Thessalonians 3:5, the same prayer goes to 'the Lord,' who directs hearts. The title the church uses for Jesus here is the one the Greek Old Testament uses for the LORD. The same comfort that Isaiah promised from God is given by Jesus.

The third point is how Christ relates to the tradition. The 'gospel' through which God called them is the message about Christ's death and resurrection, and the traditions they are to hold are above all about Him. In 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4 Paul gives the core of what he 'received and passed on': Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day. To stand firm in the tradition is to stand on the person and work of Jesus.

Finally, it is worth noting what this passage does not do. It does not make election a doctrine about a hidden decree; it ties it to Christ, in whom believers are chosen (Ephesians 1:4), and to the gospel, through which they are called. Anyone who wants to know whether he is among the chosen is sent, not to a secret list, but to Christ and the gospel. The security of the Thessalonians is the security of belonging to Him who said that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand (John 10:28).
study.god:
This paragraph is one of the clearest windows in the New Testament into the Trinitarian shape of salvation. The Lord Jesus is the one who loves (verse 13), God the Father chooses and calls, and the Spirit sanctifies. Nothing in the paragraph divides these works, as if the Father planned, the Son purchased and the Spirit applied in isolation. Together they save, and verse 16 puts the Son and the Father under one verb.

First, God is the God who acts before we do. 'From the beginning' puts His choice before any human decision and before the world's foundation (Ephesians 1:4). This does not mean God is arbitrary; Paul says He chose them out of love, as Deuteronomy 7:7 to 8 says of Israel: 'The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous.' The ground of His choice is in Himself.

Second, He is the God who finishes what He starts. Election is not left in the past: it carries through sanctification, call and glory. Paul puts this in the same breath as a command to stand, because God works through His people's perseverance. The prayer in verse 17 completes the thought: the same God who chose now 'strengthens you in every good word and deed.' The word 'every' matters: speech and action, public and private. God's work in His people is meant to reach all of life.

Third, God is the God of comfort. The 'eternal comfort' and 'good hope' given 'by grace' mark a God who consoles, not simply one who commands. Paul calls Him elsewhere 'the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort' (2 Corinthians 1:3 to 4). The comfort is not a feeling but a settled reality: it is 'eternal,' because it rests on what cannot change.

There is a tension here that the paragraph does not remove and does not try to. God's choosing is complete and prior, and yet human faith and obedience are commanded and real. Scripture holds them together without a formula, and so should we.

For worship, this means that the believer's first response is thanksgiving. Paul says 'we should always thank God for you.' Anyone who finds himself standing in grace should expect to find gratitude rather than boasting, because what he has was given. And prayer becomes the natural next step: if God is the one who strengthens, then the right way to ask for strength is to ask Him.

crossReferences.note: God chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless, and in love predestined us for adoption. This is the fuller form of Paul's 'chose you from the beginning,' adding that the choice is in Christ and that its end is holiness and sonship.

The elect are 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ.' Peter's sentence is nearly a twin of verse 13, with the Father, Spirit and Son all at work, and obedience named as the aim of sanctification.

Those God foreknew He predestined, called, justified and glorified. Paul's chain here, with chosen, set apart, called and glory, is the same movement, and Romans 8 adds that the chain is unbroken, which is the ground for the believer's confidence.

'We know that He has chosen you' because the gospel came in power, in the Holy Spirit and with great conviction. The first letter shows how the apostles recognized election: not by seeing the list, but by seeing the effect of the gospel in real lives.

Israel was chosen as a people holy to the LORD, not because of size, but because the LORD loved them. This is the Old Testament root of 'loved by the Lord' and 'chose you,' and it shows that election was always an act of love, not of merit.

Paul commends the Corinthians for 'maintaining the traditions, just as I passed them on.' It confirms that 'tradition' is a positive word for Paul when it names the apostolic teaching delivered to the church, the same sense as verse 15.

'Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.' Like verse 15, it gives a command to keep the apostolic teaching, and it adds that the keeping is done with faith and love, in Christ.

'Stand firm in the faith.' A short, rousing parallel to 'stand firm' in verse 15, spoken to a church that was divided and tempted. It shows that standing firm is the ordinary posture of the Christian life, not a crisis response.

'It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then.' The command to stand is again grounded in what Christ has done. Like 2 Thessalonians 2:15, it rests the command on a finished work, so that standing is a response to grace and not a way to earn it.

Jesus says, 'I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one.' It is the Son's own statement of what verse 14 means by sharing in His glory: the glory is a gift from the Father through the Son, and it binds the church together.

A prayer to 'our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus' with a singular verb, asking that He establish their hearts in holiness at Christ's coming. It is the first-letter version of 2 Thessalonians 2:16 to 17, showing that the pairing of Jesus and the Father in prayer was habitual for Paul.

'Comfort, comfort My people,' says your God. Paul's 'eternal comfort' belongs to this stream of promise, in which God Himself is the source of consolation for His people, now carried by the Lord Jesus and the Spirit.

God is 'the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort,' who comforts us so that we can comfort others. It uses the same family of words as 'comfort' here, and it shows that the comfort given to the church is meant to flow outward to others.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who speaks a world into being and who chooses to bless: 'God blessed them' (Genesis 1:28). The fall disrupted that blessing, and the rest of the story is the effort of God to bring a people back to Himself. This paragraph shows the shape of that effort in a few lines: God loves, God chooses, God sets apart, God calls, God gives glory. It is the whole drama of redemption in miniature, told not from the human side but from God's.

Look at what it answers from earlier in the story. In Genesis 12 God called Abram out of nothing and promised to make him a blessing. In Exodus He took a people for Himself out of slavery. Deuteronomy explains why: not their strength, but His love. Here Paul says it again of a church of Gentiles who had been strangers to the promises, and it shows that the same pattern of free choice now reaches 'all peoples,' as the promise to Abram foretold (Genesis 12:3).

Look also at what it sets up. The paragraph gives the church a calling for the long middle of the story: stand firm and hold on to the apostolic word. That is how God's people live between the call and the glory. The letter moves directly into the practical matters of chapter 3, prayer, work and discipline, showing that election is not an escape from the ordinary life of faith but the reason for it.

The story ends where this paragraph ends, in glory. 'To share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ' is the new creation in a phrase. The people who were once exiled from Eden are brought into the glory of the Son, and the comfort they are given is called 'eternal.' Hope is called 'good.' The pledge is not a feeling but a person, and the finish is certain, because the God who began the work is the one who will carry it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

For a believer today, this means that the Christian life has a starting point and an end point outside ourselves. We were loved before we loved, and we will be kept until we are glorified. Between those two fixed points, the work of the church is to hold fast to the word and to rely on the God who strengthens, one good word and one good deed at a time.

sermon.title: Chosen Before Creation for Salvation
sermon.why: In this Look at the Book study on 2 Thessalonians 2:13-17, Piper traces how God's choosing from the beginning grounds the church's assurance and its call to stand firm, showing that election works through the sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth. A careful, orthodox exposition of this movement's heart.

quiz.q: Why does Paul give thanks for the Thessalonians in verse 13?

options.text: Because God chose them from the beginning to be saved through the Spirit's sanctification and faith in the truth.
options.note: Verse 13 grounds the thanksgiving in God's electing, saving work.

options.text: Because they had chosen God by their own unaided will.
options.note: The emphasis falls on God choosing them, not on unaided human choice.

options.text: Because they had earned salvation by their good works.
options.note: Salvation here is by the Spirit and faith, not earned by works.

options.text: Because they were wealthier than the surrounding churches.
options.note: The thanksgiving concerns God's choice and their salvation, not their wealth.

quiz.q: To what did God call the Thessalonians through the gospel, according to verse 14?

options.text: That they may share in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: Verse 14 names sharing in Christ's glory as the goal of their calling.

options.text: That they may escape all responsibility to obey.
options.note: The next verse commands them to stand firm and hold the truth.

options.text: That they may gain earthly power over others.
options.note: The goal is Christ's glory, not earthly power.

options.text: That they may keep the gospel to themselves.
options.note: They are called to share Christ's glory, not to hoard the message.

quiz.q: What is Paul's central command in verse 15?

options.text: Stand firm and hold fast to the traditions the apostles taught them, by speech or letter.
options.note: Verse 15 commands steadfastness and holding the apostolic teaching.

options.text: Invent new teachings to replace what they received.
options.note: They are to cling to what was taught, not invent new doctrine.

options.text: Wait passively and do nothing at all.
options.note: Standing firm and holding the truth is active perseverance, not passivity.

options.text: Follow whatever new message seems most exciting.
options.note: The whole point is to hold the apostolic teaching against every new claim.

quiz.q: What does the command to stand firm rest upon in this passage?

options.text: God's prior choosing, calling, and saving work, which secures the church.
options.note: The therefore of verse 15 flows from God's electing and calling grace in verses 13 and 14.

options.text: The believers' own willpower and natural courage.
options.note: Their standing rests on God's choice and strengthening, not mere willpower.

options.text: Their success in avoiding all persecution.
options.note: The ground is God's grace, not freedom from hardship.

options.text: The approval of the surrounding culture.
options.note: It rests on God's choosing love, not cultural approval.

quiz.q: What does Paul pray for the church in verses 16 and 17?

options.text: That the Lord Jesus and the Father would comfort and strengthen their hearts for every good word and deed.
options.note: The benediction asks God to encourage and strengthen them by grace.

options.text: That they would be left to strengthen themselves.
options.note: The strengthening comes from the Lord and the Father, not from themselves alone.

options.text: That they would receive material riches and ease.
options.note: The prayer is for comfort, hope, and strength for good works, not riches.

options.text: That they would be freed from doing any good works.
options.note: He prays they be strengthened for every good word and deed, not freed from them.

questions: Paul roots the church's security in God choosing them from the beginning. How does knowing that your salvation began in God's love rather than your effort steady you when your faith feels shaky?
The command to stand firm rests on God's grace, not raw willpower. Where do you most need to simply keep standing in the truth right now, trusting God to hold you?
The church is told to hold fast the apostolic teaching against every deceiving message. What practices help you stay anchored in Scripture when new or exciting claims come along?
God is described as giving eternal comfort and good hope by grace. When have you felt that lasting comfort, and how might you pass it on to someone who is discouraged?
Paul prays that God would strengthen the church in every good word and deed. What specific good word or deed do you sense God strengthening you to do this week?

translationNotes.note: Chose you from the beginning renders one reading of the Greek; a footnoted alternative is God has chosen you as the firstfruits, but either way the stress is on God's electing, saving initiative.
Traditions translates paradosis, that which is handed over; the context defines it as the apostolic teaching delivered by speech or letter, not later human custom.

Our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and God our Father are named as the joint source of comfort, yet the verbs encourage and strengthen are singular, a subtle witness to the unity of the Son with the Father.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Thessalonians 2:13-17. All five verses covered contiguously.
